 At 62 He’ll Borrow $50,000 From His Own 401(k) for the Roof, Pay Himself Back at 9% Over Five Years, and the IRS Will Never Get to Call It a Withdrawal
 Borrowing from your own 401(k) at 62 sounds risky, but one short list of federal rules separates a tax-free loan from a taxable nightmare. Knowing where that line sits could save thousands before the first payment is ever made.
 By David Beren 
 Published October 24, 2026, 9:49am ET · 4 min read 
 Life After Work desk. Editor: David Beren .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 A 401(k) loan lets you borrow up to $50,000 from your own balance and repay it over five years without the IRS treating it as taxable income.
 At 9% interest, monthly payments on $50,000 run about $1,038, and all $12,275 in interest goes back into your own account.
 Leaving your job while the loan is unpaid triggers a taxable offset unless you roll the balance into an IRA by your tax filing deadline.

 If you have a 401(k) and need $50,000 for a new roof at 62, your plan can lend you the money without the IRS treating it as a withdrawal. A 401(k) loan lets you borrow from your own balance and repay yourself with interest over five years. As long as you follow a short list of federal rules, none of the cash counts as taxable income . The interest you pay also goes back into your own account.
 How a 401(k) Loan Avoids Withdrawal Treatment
 By default, any loan from your employer plan is treated as a distribution, which would make it taxable. However, one exception keeps the money a loan if it stays under the dollar caps, gets repaid within five years, and uses level payments made at least once a quarter. Meet those terms, and you owe no income tax. Every dollar of interest goes back into your own 401(k).
 Where the Rule Sits in the Tax Code
 The rule is in 26 U.S.C. § 72(p). Section 72(p)(1)(A) says a plan loan “shall be treated as having been received by such individual as a distribution”. Section 72(p)(2)(A) then removes that treatment for any loan that stays under the lower of two limits. The first is $50,000, reduced by your highest loan balance from the prior year minus whatever you still owe today.
 The second is the greater of one-half of the present value of the nonforfeitable accrued benefit (your vested balance) or $10,000. Section 72(p)(2)(B)(i) requires the loan to be “repaid within 5 years”. Section 72(p)(2)(C) requires “substantially level amortization”, which means equal payments, made at least quarterly. IRS Publication 575 lays out the same limits for qualified plans, 403(b) plans, and governmental plans.
 Who Qualifies and Who Gets Left Out
 Your plan has to offer loans, and employers can choose not to. To borrow the full amount, half of your vested balance has to reach the cap. If you had a plan loan at any point in the past 12 months, your limit shrinks.
 A longer repayment term is allowed only for a loan “used to acquire any dwelling unit” that will be your main residence. A roof on a home you already own falls outside that exception, so the five-year deadline applies. The law also bars loans taken “through the use of any credit card”.
 Steps to Borrow for the Roof
 Read your summary plan description to find the plan’s interest rate, loan fees, and how many loans you can have at once.
 Check your vested balance and any loans you’ve had in the past year so you know your real limit.
 Request a general-purpose loan with a 60-month term. At 9%, monthly payments on $50,000 are about $1,037.92, and total interest is about $12,275.07. All of that interest goes into your own account.
 Have payments taken out of your paycheck so they stay level and on time.
 Compare the rate with other options. The average credit card APR was 21.19% as of August 2026, and the 10-year Treasury yield was 5.13% on October 21, 2026.
 Fine Print That Can Turn the Loan Into Taxable Income
 Leaving your job while you still owe money is the biggest risk. If you retire or get laid off at 63, the plan usually offsets the unpaid amount against your account. Under 26 U.S.C. § 402(c)(3)(C), you have until the due date (including extensions) for filing the return of tax for the year of the offset to put the same amount into an IRA or another plan.
 This is called a rollover . If you miss that deadline, the unpaid balance counts as taxable income. A loan that defaults while you still work at the company is reported on Form 1099-R with code “L” in box 7. Since you’re older than age 59½, the 10% early withdrawal penalty doesn’t apply under Section 72(t)(2)(A)(i), but you still owe regular income tax.
 Three more costs come with the loan. You can’t deduct the interest when the loan is secured by amounts from elective deferrals, meaning the money you put into your 401(k) from your paycheck. You make payments with after-tax pay, and you pay taxes again when you withdraw it in retirement. The $50,000 also stays out of the market for five years.
 If you plan to keep working through the five-year term, the offset risk mostly goes away. If you might retire early, make sure you can cover the remaining balance before the rollover deadline.
